S6-M-Q3.skill: Use the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
S6-M-Q3.prompt: Which argument shows that every quadratic p(x) = ax² + bx + c (real a, b, c, a ≠ 0) has exactly two complex zeros, counted with multiplicity?
choices: x² - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3) has two zeros, so every quadratic has two zeros.

By the quadratic formula the zeros are (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/(2a). If b² - 4ac < 0 the square root does not exist, so there are no zeros; otherwise there are two, so a quadratic never has more than two zeros.
The graph of every quadratic is a parabola, and a parabola that opens up or down always crosses the x-axis in exactly two places, so every quadratic ax² + bx + c has exactly two zeros.
The quadratic formula (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/(2a) gives every zero: two real zeros if b² - 4ac > 0, one zero of multiplicity 2 if b² - 4ac = 0, and two non-real conjugate zeros if b² - 4ac < 0.
S6-M-Q3.correct_answer: The quadratic formula (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/(2a) gives every zero: two real zeros if b² - 4ac > 0, one zero of multiplicity 2 if b² - 4ac = 0, and two non-real conjugate zeros if b² - 4ac < 0.
S6-M-Q3.grading_note: Every case of the discriminant gives two zeros counted with multiplicity (for D < 0, √D = i√(-D) is a complex number). The others check one example, use a false graph fact (x² + 1 never crosses), or ignore complex zeros.

S6-M-Q5.skill: Use the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
S6-M-Q5.prompt: A student says p(x) = x³ + x + 1 has no zeros because it does not factor with integers. Which statement is correct?
choices: The student is right: a polynomial that does not factor over the integers has no zeros.
It has exactly 3 real zeros, because the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says a polynomial of degree 3 has 3 zeros, and a polynomial with real coefficients has only real zeros.
It has 3 complex zeros counted with multiplicity, and at least one is real, because non-real zeros of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs.
It has 3 complex zeros counted with multiplicity, and all three could be non-real, because a polynomial that does not factor over the integers need not cross the x-axis.
S6-M-Q5.correct_answer: It has 3 complex zeros counted with multiplicity, and at least one is real, because non-real zeros of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs.
S6-M-Q5.grading_note: Degree 3 gives 3 zeros (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra); conjugate pairs make the number of non-real zeros even, so at least 1 is real. The others confuse "no integer factor" with "no zero", assume all zeros are real, or ignore conjugate pairs.

S6-F2-Q1.skill: Prove existence statements about real zeros
S6-F2-Q1.prompt: Which argument proves that every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real zero?
choices: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra it has n zeros counted with multiplicity, n odd. Non-real zeros come one at a time, so there is an odd number of them, and an odd number of non-real zeros leaves at least one zero that is real.

By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra it has n zeros counted with multiplicity, n odd. Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs, so there is an even number of them; odd minus even is odd, so at least one zero is real.

The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says that every polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 with real coefficients has at least one real zero; a polynomial of odd degree has degree at least 1, so it has at least one real zero as well.
x³ - 1 has the real zero 1, so every polynomial of odd degree has a real zero.
S6-F2-Q1.correct_answer: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra it has n zeros counted with multiplicity, n odd. Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs, so there is an even number of them; odd minus even is odd, so at least one zero is real.
S6-F2-Q1.grading_note: Count zeros with the theorem and pair the non-real ones. The others check one example, misstate the theorem (it guarantees complex zeros, and x² + 1 has no real zero), or claim an odd number of non-real zeros.

S11-M-Q1.skill: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series
S11-M-Q1.prompt: Sₙ = a + ar + ar² + ... + ar^(n-1) with r ≠ 1. In the derivation of Sₙ = a(1 - rⁿ)/(1 - r), which equation results from subtracting rSₙ from Sₙ?
S11-M-Q1.grading_note: rSₙ = ar + ar² + ... + arⁿ, so every middle term cancels and Sₙ - rSₙ = a - arⁿ. Then (1 - r)Sₙ = a(1 - rⁿ), and dividing by 1 - r (allowed because r ≠ 1) gives the formula. The others use the wrong last term of rSₙ, cancel too much, or lose the first term a.

S11-M-Q2.skill: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series
S11-M-Q2.prompt: S = 3 + 6 + 12 + ... + 3 · 2⁹. With the multiply-and-subtract method, 2S - S equals which expression, and what is S?
S11-M-Q2.grading_note: 2S = 6 + 12 + ... + 3 · 2¹⁰; subtracting S leaves the last term of 2S minus the first term of S: 3 · 2¹⁰ - 3 = 3072 - 3 = 3069. The others use the wrong last term, subtract the wrong first term, or add it.

S11-M-Q3.skill: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series
S11-M-Q3.prompt: Why does the derivation of Sₙ = a(1 - rⁿ)/(1 - r) fail when r = 1, and what is Sₙ then?
choices: When r = 1 the terms a, ar, ar², ... grow without bound, so Sₙ does not exist and no formula for it is possible.
Its last step divides by 1 - r, which is 0 when r = 1. Every term then equals a, so Sₙ = na.
rSₙ cannot be formed when r = 1, so Sₙ = a.
The formula gives 0/0, which means Sₙ = 0.
S11-M-Q3.correct_answer: Its last step divides by 1 - r, which is 0 when r = 1. Every term then equals a, so Sₙ = na.
S11-M-Q3.grading_note: Division by 1 - r = 0 is not allowed; with r = 1 the series is a + a + ... + a (n terms) = na. The others treat 0/0 as 0, misread the method, or confuse r = 1 with |r| > 1.

S11-M-Q4.skill: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series
S11-M-Q4.prompt: T = 1 + x + x² + ... + xⁿ (n + 1 terms, x ≠ 1). Multiplying by x and subtracting T gives which formula? (Check: x = 2, n = 3 gives 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15.)
S11-M-Q4.grading_note: xT = x + x² + ... + x^(n+1), so xT - T = x^(n+1) - 1 and T = (x^(n+1) - 1)/(x - 1). Check: (16 - 1)/1 = 15. The others give 7, 5, and 14 for the check.

S11-M-Q5.skill: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series
S11-M-Q5.prompt: T = 100 + 100(1.05) + 100(1.05)² + ... + 100(1.05)¹⁹ (20 yearly amounts). Using the multiply-and-subtract method with 1.05T - T, which equation and total are correct? A calculator may be used.
S11-M-Q5.grading_note: 1.05T = 100(1.05) + ... + 100(1.05)²⁰, so 1.05T - T = 100(1.05)²⁰ - 100 and T = 100(1.05²⁰ - 1)/0.05 ≈ 3306.60. The others use the wrong last power (19 or 21) or forget that 1.05T - T = 0.05T.

S11-F1-Q1.skill: Prove the sum formula from a polynomial identity
S11-F1-Q1.prompt: Which argument proves the identity xⁿ - 1 = (x - 1)(x^(n-1) + x^(n-2) + ... + x + 1)?
choices: Divide both sides by x - 1 to get (xⁿ - 1)/(x - 1) = x^(n-1) + ... + x + 1; this is the geometric sum formula, so the identity is true.
x times the sum is xⁿ + x^(n-1) + ... + x; subtracting the sum x^(n-1) + ... + x + 1 cancels every term except xⁿ and -1, leaving xⁿ - 1.
x times the sum is xⁿ + x^(n-1) + ... + x; subtracting the sum x^(n-1) + ... + x + 1 cancels every term except xⁿ and 1, leaving xⁿ + 1.
For x = 2 and n = 3: 7 = 1 · 7, so the identity holds.
S11-F1-Q1.correct_answer: x times the sum is xⁿ + x^(n-1) + ... + x; subtracting the sum x^(n-1) + ... + x + 1 cancels every term except xⁿ and -1, leaving xⁿ - 1.

S15-F2-Q1.prompt: Which argument proves that the remainder when a polynomial p(x) is divided by x - a is p(a)?
choices: Write p(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r, where r is a constant because it has degree less than 1. Substituting x = a gives p(a) = 0 · q(a) + r = r.
Dividing x³ by x - 2 leaves remainder 8, and 2³ = 8, so the remainder is always p(a).
Since x - a = 0 exactly when x = a, dividing p(x) by x - a is the same as replacing x with a, so the remainder must be p(a).
Write p(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r. Substituting x = 0 gives p(0) = (0 - a)q(0) + r = -a · q(0) + r, so the remainder r equals p(a) for every a.
S15-F2-Q1.correct_answer: Write p(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r, where r is a constant because it has degree less than 1. Substituting x = a gives p(a) = 0 · q(a) + r = r.
S15-F2-Q1.grading_note: The division identity with a constant remainder, then x = a makes the factor (a - a) zero. The others check one example, substitute the wrong value (x = 0 gives p(0), not p(a)), or state the result without a reason.

S15-F2-Q2.correct_answer: The remainder has a lower degree than the divisor x - a, which has degree 1, so it has degree 0 (a constant).

S19-M-Q1.prompt: Which argument proves the identity (x² + y²)² = (x² - y²)² + (2xy)²?
choices: For x = 2 and y = 1: 25 = 9 + 16, so the identity is true.
Take the square root of both sides: x² + y² = (x² - y²) + 2xy, and the right side simplifies to x² - y² + 2xy, so the identity is true.
The left side is x⁴ + 2x²y² + y⁴. The right side is x⁴ - 2x²y² + y⁴ + 4x²y² = x⁴ + 2x²y² + y⁴. The sides are equal.
The right side is (x² - y²)² + (2xy)² = x⁴ - y⁴ + 4x²y², and the left side is x⁴ + y⁴ + 4x²y², so the two sides are equal.
S19-M-Q1.correct_answer: The left side is x⁴ + 2x²y² + y⁴. The right side is x⁴ - 2x²y² + y⁴ + 4x²y² = x⁴ + 2x²y² + y⁴. The sides are equal.
S19-M-Q1.grading_note: Both sides expand to x⁴ + 2x²y² + y⁴. The others check one example, square x² - y² as x⁴ - y⁴, or take square roots term by term.

S19-M-Q2.prompt: Which argument proves the identity a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² - ab + b²)?
choices: The product is a³ - a²b + ab² + a²b - ab² + b³. The terms -a²b and a²b cancel, ab² and -ab² cancel, leaving a³ + b³.
For a = 1 and b = 2 the left side is 1 + 8 = 9 and the right side is 3 · (1 - 2 + 4) = 9, so the identity is true for all a and b.
Multiply the first terms and the last terms: a · a² = a³ and b · b² = b³, so the product is a³ + b³.
The product is a³ - 2a²b + b³, which equals a³ + b³.
S19-M-Q2.correct_answer: The product is a³ - a²b + ab² + a²b - ab² + b³. The terms -a²b and a²b cancel, ab² and -ab² cancel, leaving a³ + b³.
S19-M-Q2.grading_note: All six products, then the cancellations. The others check one example, skip four of the six products, or multiply incorrectly.

S19-M-Q3.prompt: Which argument proves the identity (a + b)² - (a - b)² = 4ab?
choices: For a = 3 and b = 1: 16 - 4 = 12 = 4 · 3, so the identity is true.
(a² + 2ab + b²) - (a² - 2ab + b²) = a² + 2ab + b² - a² + 2ab - b² = 4ab.
(a + b)² - (a - b)² = (a² + b²) - (a² - b²) = a² + b² - a² + b² = 4ab.
S19-M-Q3.correct_answer: (a² + 2ab + b²) - (a² - 2ab + b²) = a² + 2ab + b² - a² + 2ab - b² = 4ab.
S19-M-Q3.grading_note: Subtract the whole second square, changing the sign of every term (or factor as [(a + b) - (a - b)][(a + b) + (a - b)] = (2b)(2a)). The others check one example, square binomials as a² + b², or use the false rule x² - y² = (x - y)².

S19-M-Q4.prompt: Which argument proves the identity x⁴ + 4 = (x² + 2x + 2)(x² - 2x + 2)?
choices: The right side is ((x² + 2) + 2x)((x² + 2) - 2x) = (x² + 2)² + (2x)² = x⁴ + 4x² + 4 - 4x² = x⁴ + 4.
For x = 0: 4 = 2 · 2, so the identity is true.
The right side is ((x² + 2) + 2x)((x² + 2) - 2x) = (x² + 2)² - (2x)² = x⁴ + 4x² + 4 - 4x² = x⁴ + 4.
Multiply the first terms and the last terms: x² · x² = x⁴ and 2 · 2 = 4.
S19-M-Q4.correct_answer: The right side is ((x² + 2) + 2x)((x² + 2) - 2x) = (x² + 2)² - (2x)² = x⁴ + 4x² + 4 - 4x² = x⁴ + 4.
S19-M-Q4.grading_note: Group as a difference of squares (or expand all nine products). The others check one example, use (u + v)(u - v) = u² + v², or skip the middle products.

S19-M-Q5.prompt: Which argument proves the identity (n + 1)³ - n³ = 3n² + 3n + 1?

S19-M-Q5.grading_note: Expand (n + 1)³ correctly and subtract. The others check several values (evidence, not a proof) or use the false rules a³ - b³ = (a - b)³ and (n + 1)³ = n³ + 1.

S19-F2-Q1.skill: Prove identities with the Binomial Theorem
S19-F2-Q1.prompt: Which argument uses the Binomial Theorem to prove that the entries in row n of Pascal's Triangle add to 2ⁿ?
choices: Row n has n + 1 entries, and each entry is the sum of the two entries above it, so every row has twice as many entries as the row before it and the sum of row n is 2ⁿ.
Row 3 is 1, 3, 3, 1, which adds to 8 = 2³, so every row n adds to 2ⁿ.
Set x = y = 1 in (x + y)ⁿ = C(n, 0)xⁿ + C(n, 1)xⁿ⁻¹y + ... + C(n, n)yⁿ. The left side is 2ⁿ and the right side is C(n, 0) + C(n, 1) + ... + C(n, n), the row sum.
Set x = 1 and y = 0 in (x + y)ⁿ = C(n, 0)xⁿ + ... + C(n, n)yⁿ: the left side is 1 and the right side is C(n, 0) = 1, so each row adds to 2ⁿ.
S19-F2-Q1.correct_answer: Set x = y = 1 in (x + y)ⁿ = C(n, 0)xⁿ + C(n, 1)xⁿ⁻¹y + ... + C(n, n)yⁿ. The left side is 2ⁿ and the right side is C(n, 0) + C(n, 1) + ... + C(n, n), the row sum.
S19-F2-Q1.grading_note: Substituting 1 for x and y makes every term equal to its coefficient. The others check one row, use a substitution that gives 1, or argue from the number of entries.

S37-M-Q1.skill: Explain the extension of sine and cosine to all real numbers
S37-M-Q1.prompt: Which statement correctly explains how the unit circle defines cos t and sin t for every real number t?
choices: Start at (0, 1) and travel t units clockwise; cos t is the y-coordinate and sin t is the x-coordinate of the endpoint.
Start at (1, 0) and travel |t| units along the unit circle, counterclockwise if t > 0 and clockwise if t < 0; cos t and sin t are the x- and y-coordinates of the endpoint.

Draw a right triangle with an acute angle of t radians; cos t and sin t are the ratios adjacent/hypotenuse and opposite/hypotenuse, so the definition works only for t between 0 and π/2.

S37-M-Q2.skill: Explain the extension of sine and cosine to all real numbers
S37-M-Q2.prompt: Which explanation shows why sin(t + 2π) = sin t for every real number t?
choices: For t = π/2 both sides equal 1, so they are always equal.
Sine distributes over addition, so sin(t + 2π) = sin t + sin 2π, and sin 2π = 0 because the point at 2π is (1, 0); therefore sin(t + 2π) = sin t.
Adding 2π to t reflects the endpoint on the unit circle over the x-axis, and a reflection over the x-axis keeps the y-coordinate, so sin(t + 2π) = sin t.
The unit circle has circumference 2π, so adding 2π adds one full trip around it: t and t + 2π end at the same point, which has the same y-coordinate.
S37-M-Q2.correct_answer: The unit circle has circumference 2π, so adding 2π adds one full trip around it: t and t + 2π end at the same point, which has the same y-coordinate.
S37-M-Q2.grading_note: One full turn returns to the same point. The others distribute sine over a sum (false in general), check one value, or describe the wrong motion.

choices: For θ = π/2: (1 - 0)(1 + 0) = 1 = sin²(π/2), so the identity holds.
(1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 - 2cos θ + cos²θ, and by the Pythagorean identity this equals sin²θ.
(1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 - cos²θ, and 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ by the Pythagorean identity.
(1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 + cos²θ, which equals sin²θ.
S40-F1-Q2.correct_answer: (1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 - cos²θ, and 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ by the Pythagorean identity.
S40-F1-Q2.grading_note: Multiply (difference of squares), then use the identity. The others multiply incorrectly or check one angle.

S40-F1-Q5.skill: Prove identities derived from the Pythagorean identity
choices: Replace sin²θ with 1 - cos²θ: cos²θ - (1 - cos²θ) = cos²θ - 1 + cos²θ = 2cos²θ - 1.
Add sin²θ to both sides to get cos²θ = 2cos²θ - 1 + sin²θ, which is always true.
For θ = 0: 1 - 0 = 2 - 1, so the identity holds.
Replace sin²θ with 1 - cos²θ: cos²θ - 1 - cos²θ = -1, so the identity is false for every θ.
S40-F1-Q5.correct_answer: Replace sin²θ with 1 - cos²θ: cos²θ - (1 - cos²θ) = cos²θ - 1 + cos²θ = 2cos²θ - 1.
S40-F1-Q5.grading_note: Substitute sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ and subtract the whole expression. The others drop the parentheses, check one angle, or end with an unproved statement.

S57-F1-Q1.skill: Reason about sums and products of even and odd functions
S57-F1-Q1.prompt: Which argument proves that the sum of two odd functions f and g is odd?
choices: x³ and x⁵ are odd and x³ + x⁵ is odd, so every sum of two odd functions is odd.
(f + g)(-x) = f(x) + g(x) = (f + g)(x), so the sum is odd.
(f + g)(-x) = -f(-x) - g(-x) = -(f + g)(-x), so the sum is odd.
S57-F1-Q1.grading_note: Use f(-x) = -f(x) and g(-x) = -g(x), then factor out -1. The others use the even-function rule (and would show even), check one example, or misapply the definition.

S57-F1-Q2.skill: Reason about sums and products of even and odd functions
S57-F1-Q2.prompt: Which argument proves that the product of two odd functions f and g is even?
choices: x · x³ = x⁴ is even, so every product of two odd functions is even.
Odd times odd is odd for whole numbers, so the product of two odd functions is odd.
(fg)(-x) = f(-x)g(-x) = -f(x)g(x), so the product is odd.
S57-F1-Q2.grading_note: The two negative signs multiply to +1. The others drop one negative sign, check one example, or confuse odd functions with odd numbers.

S81-M-Q1.skill: Derive values from special triangles and relate π - x, π + x, 2π - x to x
S81-M-Q1.prompt: A 30°-60°-90° triangle with hypotenuse 1 is half of an equilateral triangle with side 1. Which derivation of sin(π/3) and cos(π/3) is correct?
choices: The short leg is 1/2 and the long leg is √(1 - 1/4) = √3/2. The angle π/3 is opposite the long leg, so sin(π/3) = √3/2 and cos(π/3) = 1/2.
The long leg is √(1 + 1/4) = √5/2, so sin(π/3) = √5/2.
The short leg is 1/2 and the long leg is √(1 - 1/4) = √3/2. The angle π/3 is opposite the short leg, so sin(π/3) = 1/2 and cos(π/3) = √3/2.
The legs are 1/2 and 1 - 1/2 = 1/2, so sin(π/3) = cos(π/3) = 1/2.
S81-M-Q1.correct_answer: The short leg is 1/2 and the long leg is √(1 - 1/4) = √3/2. The angle π/3 is opposite the long leg, so sin(π/3) = √3/2 and cos(π/3) = 1/2.
S81-M-Q1.grading_note: Halving the base gives 1/2; the Pythagorean Theorem gives √3/2; the larger angle is opposite the longer leg. The others put π/3 opposite the short leg, subtract lengths instead of using the Pythagorean Theorem, or add instead of subtracting squares.

The legs are 1 and √2, so tan(π/4) = opposite/adjacent = 1/√2 = √2/2.
The two legs are equal, so tan(π/4) = opposite/adjacent = 1.
S81-M-Q2.correct_answer: The two legs are equal, so tan(π/4) = opposite/adjacent = 1.
S81-M-Q2.grading_note: Equal legs make the ratio 1. The others use the hypotenuse as a leg, add instead of dividing, or use a 30°-60°-90° fact.

S81-F1-Q1.prompt: Which derivation of tan(π/6) from a special triangle is correct?
choices: The opposite side is half the hypotenuse, so tan(π/6) = 1/2.
In the 30°-60°-90° triangle with hypotenuse 1, π/6 is opposite the leg 1/2 and adjacent to the leg √3/2, so tan(π/6) = (1/2)/(√3/2) = 1/√3 = √3/3.
In the 30°-60°-90° triangle with hypotenuse 1, π/6 is opposite the leg √3/2 and adjacent to the leg 1/2, so tan(π/6) = (√3/2)/(1/2) = √3 exactly.
S81-F1-Q1.correct_answer: In the 30°-60°-90° triangle with hypotenuse 1, π/6 is opposite the leg 1/2 and adjacent to the leg √3/2, so tan(π/6) = (1/2)/(√3/2) = 1/√3 = √3/3.
S81-F1-Q1.grading_note: Opposite over adjacent, then simplify (1/2)/(√3/2) = 1/√3 = √3/3. The others use the angle π/3, give sin(π/6) instead, or simplify the quotient incorrectly.

S81-F1-Q2.skill: Derive more special values and the reflection identities
S81-F1-Q2.prompt: Which unit-circle argument explains why cos(π - x) = -cos x?
choices: The points for x and π - x are reflections of each other over the y-axis, so their x-coordinates (the cosines) are opposites.
cos(π - π/3) = -1/2 = -cos(π/3), so the rule always holds.
cos(π - x) = cos π - cos x = -1 - cos x.
The points for x and π - x are reflections of each other over the x-axis, so their x-coordinates (the cosines) are opposites.
S81-F1-Q2.correct_answer: The points for x and π - x are reflections of each other over the y-axis, so their x-coordinates (the cosines) are opposites.
S81-F1-Q2.grading_note: Reflection over the y-axis changes the sign of x and keeps y. The others name the wrong reflection (it keeps x), distribute cosine over a difference, or check one value.

S82-M-Q1.skill: Explain the symmetry and periodicity of trigonometric functions with the unit circle
S82-M-Q1.prompt: Which unit-circle explanation shows why sin(-x) = -sin x?
choices: The points for x and -x are (a, b) and (-a, b), reflections of each other over the y-axis, so their sines are opposites.
sin(-π/6) = -1/2 = -sin(π/6), so the rule always holds.
The points for x and -x are (a, b) and (a, -b), reflections over the x-axis, so the sines b and -b are opposites.
A negative sign can always be moved outside a function, so sin(-x) = -sin x.
S82-M-Q1.correct_answer: The points for x and -x are (a, b) and (a, -b), reflections over the x-axis, so the sines b and -b are opposites.
S82-M-Q1.grading_note: Equal arcs in opposite directions from (1, 0) give points that mirror over the x-axis. The others name the wrong reflection, use a false general rule (cos(-x) = cos x, not -cos x), or check one value.

S82-M-Q2.skill: Explain the symmetry and periodicity of trigonometric functions with the unit circle
S82-M-Q2.prompt: Which unit-circle explanation shows why cos(x + 2π) = cos x?
choices: Adding 2π moves the point to the opposite side of the unit circle, and opposite points on the circle have the same x-coordinate, so the cosine is the same.
cos(x + 2π) = cos x + cos 2π = cos x + 1.
Adding 2π travels one full turn around the unit circle and ends at the same point, so the x-coordinate (the cosine) is the same.
cos(0 + 2π) = 1 = cos 0, so the rule always holds.
S82-M-Q2.correct_answer: Adding 2π travels one full turn around the unit circle and ends at the same point, so the x-coordinate (the cosine) is the same.
S82-M-Q2.grading_note: The circumference is 2π, so x and x + 2π give the same point. The others distribute cosine over a sum, describe the wrong motion, or check one value.

S82-M-Q3.skill: Explain the symmetry and periodicity of trigonometric functions with the unit circle
S82-M-Q3.prompt: Which unit-circle explanation shows why tan(x + π) = tan x?
choices: Adding π gives the point (a, -b), a reflection over the x-axis, so tan(x + π) = -b/a = -tan x, which is not tan x.
Adding π gives the opposite point (-a, -b) of (a, b), and tan = (-b)/(-a) = b/a, the same ratio.
Adding π travels a full turn, so the point is the same.
tan(π/4 + π) = 1 = tan(π/4), so the rule always holds.
S82-M-Q3.correct_answer: Adding π gives the opposite point (-a, -b) of (a, b), and tan = (-b)/(-a) = b/a, the same ratio.
S82-M-Q3.grading_note: Half a turn takes (a, b) to (-a, -b); both coordinates change sign, so the ratio is unchanged. The others use the wrong point, mistake π for a full turn, or check one value.
